title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks
author: Ava Johnson
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, known issues, release notes summary, and operational runbooks for the Serving Runtime team. It is intended for engineers (runtime, infra, SRE), performance reviewers, and on-call responders.

Goals
- Provide a single reference for architecture and operational practices.
- Describe kernel scheduling decisions and how they map to workload classes.
- Standardize profiling, benchmark, and perf-regression workflows.
- Include actionable runbooks for common incidents and maintenance tasks.

Owners and Contacts
- Primary owner: runtime-platform@redwood.internal (Runtime Platform team)
- Runbook and oncall owner: eng-sre@redwood.internal
- Component leads:
  - CPU/GEMM & quantization: Ravi Patel
  - Kernel scheduler & batching: Marta López
  - Profiling & benchmarks: Chen Wei

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Summary
The Serving Runtime provides GPU- and CPU-based inference hosting with the following core components: request router, model manager, execution engine, KV cache, batching layer, telemetry/observability, and optional compilation/graph optimizer. The runtime is modular to support hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Key components
- Request Router: routes requests by policy (latency, cost, region, model-compatibility). Support for model variants and fallbacks.
- Model Manager: model artifacts, version pins, quantization profile selection, and warm cache orchestration.
- Execution Engine: device abstraction (CUDA, ROCm, XPU), kernel registry, and execution planner.
- Kernel Scheduler: maps inference tasks (micro-batches, KV cache hits, long-context continuations) onto GPU/CPU resources. See section 2 for design.
- Batcher: continuous batching that groups compatible requests while honoring per-request latency budgets.
- KV Cache Service: shared per-model KV cache with TTL, shard-aware eviction, and prefix caching.
- Observability: token-level tracing, tail-latency histograms, per-model QPS/cost counters, and perf events.

SLOs and targets
- 99th percentile (p99) token latency target for small-chat workloads: 120ms (hosted tier), 90ms (dedicated).
- Average tokens/sec per GPU (gpt-like workload): baseline varies by model; maintain +/- 10% of curated profile.
- On-call MTTR for production GPU OOM incidents: < 45 minutes.

2) Kernel scheduling: design and operational rules

Design principles
- Priority classes: latency-critical, throughput-optimized, background/batch.
- Preemption: latency-critical requests can preempt throughput jobs; preemption is cooperative via checkpointable kernel slices.
- Resource accounting: track per-tenant memory reservations and per-workload compute weights to avoid noisy neighbor effects.

Scheduler components and policies
- Admission controller: evaluates incoming request budgets, model size, and current device utilization before admitting to queue.
- Work queues: separate queues per priority class and per-device partition (e.g., small-model lane, large-model lane).
- Slice-based execution: long kernels are split into small slices (default 32ms) to enable preemption and fairness.
- Greedy packing: within throughput lane, scheduler packs sequences with matching kernel shapes to increase kernel fusion and reduce launch overhead.

Operational knobs (config table)
| Setting | Default | Notes |
| admission.max_concurrency_per_gpu | 64 | Soft limit enforced by admission controller |
| scheduler.slice_ms | 32 | Max time slice for cooperative preemption |
| packing.shape_similarity_threshold | 0.85 | Cosine similarity threshold for kernel fusion packing |
| eviction.kv_ttl_sec | 7200 | Default TTL for model KV cache entries |

Tuning guidance
- For low-latency workloads reduce scheduler.slice_ms to 16ms and enable strict preemption. Monitor throughput impact.
- For throughput-focused queues increase admission.max_concurrency_per_gpu and packing.threshold to improve utilization.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

When to profile
- New model added to catalog
- Model version rollout with quantization change
- Unexpected CPU/GPU regressions or U-shaped tail latencies

Tools and traces
- perf-trace: distributed trace collector that aggregates device traces, kernel launches, and runtime events.
- nvprof/nvtx (CUDA): for low-level kernel timing (used in dedicated perf labs).
- psutil and nvidia-smi snapshots for resource baselines.
- perfkit benchmarks (see section 4).

Procedure (step-by-step)
1. Reproduce with representative workloads in the staging perf cluster. Capture request traces for 30 minutes.
2. Record tail-latency histograms and identify correlated kernel launches using perf-trace.
3. For top-k problematic kernels, capture nvprof traces in a dedicated job and annotate with nvtx markers:

   ```bash
   # staging job wrapper
   export NVTX_ENABLE=1
   nvprof --log-file kernel-trace.txt --profile-child-processes -- 
     ./runtime_perf_job --model my-model --qps 50 --seq-len 1024
   ```

4. Compare kernel timings to the model's reference profile and inspect for increased memcpy/serialization overhead.
5. If serialization or scheduling delays dominate, inspect batching logs and slice boundaries (look for frequent preemption markers).

Common findings and actions
- High memcpy time: enable pinned-memory pooling and increase io-thread count.
- Frequent preemptions causing thrashing: raise scheduler.slice_ms or adjust admission weights for affected tenant.
- Kernel launch overhead: enable packing by increasing shape_similarity_threshold or use kernel fusion flags during compilation.

4) Benchmarking suite and regression process

Benchmark suite components
- perfkit: core harness to replay synthetic and recorded traffic, produce token-latency histograms and resource counters.
- model-profiles: curated model inputs, typical sequence length distributions, and golden throughput numbers.
- nightly-regressions: CI job that runs the suite across critical instance types and reports diffs.

How to run locally (quickstart)
- Checkout repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood/runtime-perf.git
- Run a single-model benchmark:

   ```bash
   cd runtime-perf
   ./bin/run_benchmark --model=gpt-medium --instance=gpu-v100 --qps=20 --duration=600
   ```

Acceptance criteria for changes
- No >5% degradation in median latency and no >10% degradation in p99 for the affected model families.
- CPU/GPU memory usage must stay within +/-8% of baseline unless explicitly approved.

Regression triage
- If nightly job flags a regression, open a perf-triage ticket and assign to profiling owner. Attach traces, diffs, and relevant commit range. Use the regression-triage template.

5) Release notes (runtime-specific summary guidance)

Each runtime release must include a short release-notes section with:
- Summary of major changes (kernel updates, scheduler changes, memory accounting, batching changes).
- Benchmark summary (tabular: models tested, median/p99 deltas).
- Migration notes for Dedicated/Private customers (config flags, compatibility).
- Known risks and recommended mitigations.

Example release note snippet
- Version: v2027.05.10
- Highlights: cooperative preemption improved fairness; packing algorithm introduced shape-based fusion; default scheduler.slice_ms reduced from 48ms to 32ms.
- Benchmarks: median latency change (gpt-medium) +0.8%, p99 -1.2% (improvement).

6) Known issues (current)

- Issue: rare GPU OOM during large-context multimodal requests
  - Symptom: single tenant job fails with OOM while other queues idle.
  - Mitigation: immediate action: reduce admission.max_concurrency_per_gpu for affected tenant and evict cold KV entries. Persistent fix: increase per-tenant memory reservation or enable model sharding.
- Issue: tail-latency spikes on packed batches after quantization changes
  - Symptom: p99 increases by 25% when quantized weights are used for certain attention kernels.
  - Mitigation: rollback quantization profile, run nvprof, and file model-onboarding ticket.

7) Runbooks (on-call playbooks)

Incident: p99 token latency spike for hosted chat API
1. Confirm alert details and scope in PagerDuty. Identify affected model(s) and regions.
2. Pull last 15m traces from perf-trace and compare kernel launch frequency.
3. Check admission queue lengths and device utilization dashboards (Grafana).
4. If queues backlogged and preemption markers visible: temporarily increase scheduler.slice_ms to 64ms for the cluster and observe.
5. If OOMs observed on GPUs: trigger tenant eviction (evict low-priority throughput jobs) and scale up dedicated nodes if autoscale available.
6. Open incident ticket and run triage playbook (link to postmortem template).

Maintenance: kernel rollout checklist
1. Run unit and integration tests on runtime repo.
2. Run full perfkit suite in perf staging cluster and compare to baseline.
3. Deploy to canary pool (5% of traffic) with continuous tracing enabled for 2 hours.
4. If no regressions, progressively increase to 25% and then 100% per normal rollout schedule.
5. Record release notes and notify impacted customers in Dedicated/Private channels.

Appendices
A. Useful CLI snippets
- Dump admission state: 
  ```bash
  curl -sS http://localhost:8001/admin/admission/status | jq
  ```
- Trigger KV cache eviction for model: 
  ```bash
  curl -X POST 
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
    http://localhost:8001/admin/cache/evict 
    -d '{"model":"my-model","threshold":"lru"}'
  ```
